framework: AP Macroeconomics Course and Exam Description (effective fall 2026)
subject: Macroeconomics

source.licence: © College Board; structure + our own wording only

outcomes.text: Define scarcity and economic resources.
Explain that scarce resources force individuals and societies to make choices.
Define the production possibilities curve and use it to show opportunity cost, tradeoffs, efficiency and growth, and calculate opportunity cost.
Describe the PPC as a model of tradeoffs in allocating resources.
Use the PPC to illustrate scarcity, opportunity cost, efficiency, unused resources and growth or contraction.
Relate the PPC's shape to constant, increasing or decreasing opportunity costs.
Explain that the PPC shifts with changes in factors of production or technology.
Show that economic growth shifts the PPC outward.

topics.title: 1.3 Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade

subtopics.title: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade

outcomes.text: Define and determine absolute and comparative advantage from data.
Define absolute advantage as producing more with the same resources.
Define comparative advantage as producing at lower opportunity cost.
Explain how specialization by comparative advantage creates gains from trade and calculate mutually beneficial terms of trade.
Explain how specialization and exchange allow consumption beyond the PPC.
Show that opportunity costs set the range of terms of trade that benefit both sides.
Define the law of demand and explain the price and quantity demanded relationship.
State the inverse price and quantity demanded relationship giving a downward-sloping demand curve.
Explain the determinants of demand.
Show that factors like income shift the market demand curve.
Define the law of supply and explain the price and quantity supplied relationship.
State the positive price and quantity supplied relationship giving an upward-sloping supply curve.
Explain the determinants of supply.
Show that factors like input prices shift the market supply curve.
Define market equilibrium using graphs.
Find equilibrium at the price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
Define surplus and shortage, explain price adjustment and calculate imbalances.
Explain that market forces push prices toward equilibrium when there are surpluses or shortages.
Explain how demand and supply changes alter equilibrium price and quantity.
Show that changes in determinants of supply or demand give a new equilibrium.

units.title: Unit 2: Economic Indicators and the Business Cycle

outcomes.text: Define how GDP is measured and its components using the circular flow, and calculate nominal GDP.
Describe GDP as a measure of the economy's final output.
Represent GDP as a flow of income and expenditure in the circular flow diagram.
Name the expenditures, income and value-added ways of measuring GDP.
Define the limitations of GDP.
Explain that GDP is useful but misses things like nonmarket transactions.
Define the labor force, unemployment rate and participation rate, explain what moves them, and calculate them.
Define the unemployment rate as the share of the labor force without work.
Define the labor force participation rate as the share of adults in the labor force.
Define the limitations of the unemployment rate.
Explain why the rate can understate joblessness by excluding discouraged and part-time workers.
Define types of unemployment and the natural rate, and explain changes in them.
Distinguish cyclical, frictional and structural unemployment.
Define the natural rate as frictional plus structural unemployment at full-employment output.
Identify cyclical unemployment as the gap between actual and natural rates.
Explain that the natural rate drifts over time with labor force changes.
Define CPI, inflation, deflation, disinflation and real variables, use price indices to compare over time, and calculate CPI, inflation and real changes.
Describe the CPI as the income needed to keep the same living standard under new prices.
Describe the CPI as the cost of a fixed basket relative to a base year.
Calculate the inflation rate as the percentage change in a price index like CPI or the GDP deflator.
Deflate nominal variables by the price level to get real variables.
Define the shortcomings of the CPI as a measure of inflation.
Explain that substitution bias makes the CPI overstate true inflation.
Explain the costs of unexpected inflation or deflation to individuals and the economy.
Explain how unexpected inflation redistributes wealth, such as from lenders to borrowers.
Define nominal and real GDP.
Contrast nominal GDP as spending on output with real GDP as amount produced.
Contrast current-price and constant-price measures of output.
Calculate real GDP and the GDP deflator.
Describe base-year-price real GDP and why it can overstate growth.
Convert nominal GDP to real GDP with the GDP deflator.
Define and explain turning points and phases of the business cycle using graphs and data.
Describe business cycles as output and employment swings from aggregate supply or demand changes.
Name the phases as recession and expansion.
Name the turning points as peak and trough.
Define the output gap as actual minus potential output.
Equate potential output with full-employment output at the natural unemployment rate.

units.title: Unit 3: National Income and Price Determination

outcomes.text: Define the AD curve and explain its slope and determinants.
Describe AD as price level versus total demand from households, firms, government and the rest of the world.
Explain AD's downward slope by the real wealth, interest rate and exchange rate effects.
Show that non-price-level changes in AD components shift the AD curve.
Define the expenditure and tax multipliers, MPC and MPS, and calculate how spending and tax changes move real GDP.
Explain that a $1 autonomous spending change triggers further spending and output changes.
Use the expenditure multiplier to size an AD change from a component change.
Use the tax multiplier to size an AD change from a tax change.
Show that both multipliers depend on the marginal propensity to consume.
Define MPC as change in consumption over change in disposable income, with MPC plus MPS equal to one.
Define the SRAS curve and explain its slope and determinants.
Describe SRAS as price level versus quantity of output supplied.
Explain SRAS's upward slope by sticky wages and prices.
Show that production cost changes, such as inflation expectations, shift SRAS.
Explain how moving along SRAS links the price level to unemployment.
Explain the short-run tradeoff between inflation and unemployment along SRAS.
Define the short run and the long run.
Contrast fixed short-run input prices with flexible long-run wages and prices, and note no long-run inflation-unemployment tradeoff.
Define the LRAS curve.
Link LRAS to the PPC as maximum sustainable capacity.
Explain why LRAS is vertical at full-employment output.
Explain short-run and long-run equilibrium price level and output using graphs.
Locate short-run equilibrium where AD meets SRAS.
Locate long-run equilibrium where AD and SRAS meet on LRAS.
Show short-run output above, at or below full employment as inflationary or recessionary gaps.

topics.title: 3.6 Changes in the AD-AS Model in the Short Run

subtopics.title: Changes in the AD-AS Model in the Short Run

outcomes.text: Explain short-run output, employment and price level responses to AD or AS shocks.
Show a positive or negative AD shock moves output, employment and prices the same way.
Show a positive or negative SRAS shock moves output and employment opposite to prices.
Distinguish demand-pull from cost-push inflation.
Explain long-run responses of output, employment and prices to AD or AS shocks.
Explain how flexible wages and prices restore full employment without policy.
Interpret LRAS shifts as changes in full-employment output and growth.
Define fiscal policy, explain and calculate its short-run effects using graphs.
State that governments use fiscal policy for goals such as full employment.
Name government spending and taxes/transfers as fiscal tools.
Contrast direct spending effects with indirect tax and transfer effects on AD.
Explain that the spending multiplier exceeds the tax multiplier.
Match expansionary or contractionary policy to recessionary or inflationary gaps.
Describe fiscal policy effects on AD, real output and prices.
Use the AD-AS model to show short-run fiscal effects.
Define why discretionary fiscal policy has lags.
Explain that deciding on and implementing policy takes time.
Define automatic stabilizers and explain how they moderate business cycles.
Explain that stabilizers support recessions and cool overheated expansions.
Show tax revenue falling automatically with GDP to cushion consumption.
Show tax revenue rising automatically with GDP to slow consumption.
Identify transfer payments from social programs as automatic stabilizers.
Define liquidity, return and risk of financial assets including money, and explain how bond prices relate to interest rates.
Identify cash and demand deposits as the most liquid money.
Name bonds and stocks as alternatives to holding liquid money.
Show that prices of previously issued bonds move inversely to interest rates.
Define the opportunity cost of holding money as forgone interest on other assets.
Define nominal and real interest rates, relate them to expected inflation, and calculate them.
Define the nominal rate as the loan rate unadjusted for inflation.
Set nominal rates as expected real rate plus expected inflation.
Compute a real rate afterwards as nominal rate minus actual inflation.

topics.title: 4.3 Definition, Measurement, and Functions of Money

subtopics.title: Definition, Measurement, and Functions of Money

outcomes.text: Define money and its functions and calculate measures of money.
Define money as any asset accepted as payment.
List money's roles as medium of exchange, unit of account and store of value.
Measure the money supply with M1 and M2.
Define the monetary base as currency in circulation plus bank reserves.

topics.title: 4.4 Banking and the Expansion of the Money Supply

subtopics.title: Banking and the Expansion of the Money Supply

outcomes.text: Define banking terms, explain how banks create money, and calculate effects using balance sheets.
Show how banks organize assets and liabilities on balance sheets.
Describe fractional reserve banking.
Split reserves into required and excess reserves.
Explain that excess reserves are the basis for money expansion.
Define the money multiplier as money supply over monetary base.
Show that money supply expansion depends on the money multiplier.
Calculate the maximum money multiplier as the reciprocal of the required reserve ratio.
Explain why the simple multiplier can overstate expansion when banks hold excess reserves or people hold cash.
Define the money market, money demand and supply, and explain how the nominal rate relates to quantity demanded.
Show money demand as an inverse relation between nominal interest rate and money held.
Explain that money supply is independent of the rate, set by the central bank's base.
Define money market equilibrium.
Find equilibrium where the nominal rate equates money demanded and supplied.
Explain how nominal interest rates adjust to restore money market equilibrium.
Show that disequilibrium rates create surpluses or shortages that push rates to equilibrium.
Explain determinants of money demand and supply and their effect on the equilibrium rate.
Show how price level or monetary policy shifts change the equilibrium nominal rate.
Define monetary policy, explain and calculate its short-run effects using graphs and balance sheets.
State that central banks pursue goals such as price stability.
Name tools: discount and administered rates, open market operations and reserve ratio, and how they differ with limited versus ample reserves.
Explain that open-market purchases raise reserves and the base, and sales lower them.
Explain that with limited reserves, open-market operations affect money supply more than the base through the multiplier.
Describe central bank targeting of an overnight policy rate such as the federal funds rate.
Explain how central banks influence nominal rates, and so investment and consumption, differently with limited or ample reserves.
Use expansionary or contractionary policy to close recessionary or inflationary gaps.
Describe monetary policy effects on rates, AD, output and prices.
Use the money market, reserve market or AD-AS model to show short-run policy effects.
Define why monetary policy has lags.
Explain lags from recognizing problems and from economic adjustment to policy.
Define the loanable funds market and its demand and supply, and explain their link to the real interest rate.
Describe the market as the behavior of savers and borrowers.
Show that demand for loanable funds falls as the real rate rises.
Show that supply of loanable funds rises as the real rate rises.
Define national savings in closed and open economies.
Compute closed-economy national savings as public plus private savings.
Explain that open-economy investment equals national savings plus net capital inflow.
Define loanable funds market equilibrium.
Find equilibrium where the real rate equates funds demanded and supplied.
Explain how real interest rates adjust to restore loanable funds equilibrium.
Show that surpluses or shortages push real rates to equilibrium.
Explain determinants of loanable funds demand and supply and their effects on the real rate and quantity.
Use the market to show effects of government spending, taxes and borrowing on interest rates.
Show how shifts like an investment tax credit or saving changes alter the rate and quantity.

units.title: Unit 5: Long-Run Consequences of Stabilization Policies

topics.title: 5.1 Fiscal and Monetary Policy Actions in the Short Run

subtopics.title: Fiscal and Monetary Policy Actions in the Short Run

outcomes.text: Explain the effects of combined fiscal and monetary policy actions using graphs.
Combine fiscal and monetary policy to restore full employment in either gap.
Describe combined policy effects on AD, output, prices and interest rates.
Define the short-run and long-run Phillips curves and explain equilibrium in the model.
Show the short-run inflation-unemployment tradeoff on the downward-sloping SRPC.
State that an economy always operates somewhere along the SRPC.
Draw the LRPC vertical at the natural rate of unemployment.
Locate long-run equilibrium where SRPC and LRPC intersect.
Read points left of equilibrium as inflationary gaps and right as recessionary gaps.
Explain unemployment and inflation responses in the short and long run.
Treat demand shocks as movements along the SRPC.
Treat supply shocks as shifts of the SRPC.
Shift the LRPC when the natural rate changes.
Explain inflation as a monetary phenomenon, define the quantity theory and calculate with it.
Explain that inflation comes from sustained, too-rapid money supply growth.
Show that at full employment money supply changes do not affect long-run real output.
Use the quantity theory to tie money growth to the inflation rate.

topics.title: 5.4 Government Deficits and the National Debt

subtopics.title: Government Deficits and the National Debt

outcomes.text: Define budget surplus or deficit and national debt, and explain the debt's burden.
Define the deficit as tax revenue minus purchases plus transfers in a year.
Explain that deficits add to the national debt.
Explain that interest on debt grows the debt and crowds out other uses of funds.
Define crowding out and explain how fiscal policy can cause it.
Explain that deficit governments typically borrow to finance spending.
Use the loanable funds model to show borrowing raising the real rate and crowding out investment.
Define crowding out as lower interest-sensitive private spending from government borrowing.
Explain that crowding out can lower capital accumulation and long-run growth.
Define measures and determinants of economic growth, explain them, and calculate per capita GDP and growth.
Measure growth as growth in real GDP per capita.
Relate employment and output through the aggregate production function.
Define average labor productivity as output per employed worker.
Name technology and physical and human capital per worker as productivity determinants.
Show output per capita rising with physical and human capital per capita.
Explain how the PPC is related to the LRAS curve.
Equate an outward PPC shift with a rightward LRAS shift.
Explain public policies for long-run growth and define supply-side fiscal policies.
Show that policies affecting productivity and labor participation change real GDP per capita.
Explain that infrastructure and technology investment affects growth.
Explain supply-side policy effects on AD, AS and potential output through incentives.

units.title: Unit 6: Open Economy: International Trade and Finance

outcomes.text: Define the current account, capital and financial account and balance of payments, explain and calculate them.
Describe the current account as net exports, net foreign income and net transfers.
Recognize that the current account and trade balance may be in surplus or deficit.
Describe the capital and financial account as capital transfers and asset trades.
Interpret CFA surplus as capital inflow and deficit as outflow.
Define the balance of payments as the record of international transactions made of the CA and CFA.
Treat money inflows as credits and outflows as debits so CA plus CFA equals zero.
Define exchange rate, appreciation and depreciation, and calculate relative currency values.
Define the exchange rate as the price of one currency in another.
Define appreciation and depreciation as a currency gaining or losing value.
Define the foreign exchange market and currency demand and supply, and explain their relation to the exchange rate.
Explain that currency demand arises from demand for a country's goods and assets and slopes downward.
Explain that currency supply arises from payments in other currencies and slopes upward.
Define the equilibrium exchange rate.
Find equilibrium where quantities of the currency demanded and supplied are equal.
Explain how exchange rates adjust to restore equilibrium.
Show that surpluses and shortages push exchange rates to equilibrium.

topics.title: 6.4 Policies and Conditions in the Foreign Exchange Market

subtopics.title: Policies and Conditions in the Foreign Exchange Market

outcomes.text: Explain determinants of currency demand and supply and how shifts change the exchange rate.
Show how shifts such as demand for goods or tariffs change the exchange rate.
Explain that fiscal policy can influence AD, output, prices and exchange rates.
Explain that monetary policy works through interest rates to affect exchange rates.

topics.title: 6.5 Changes in the Foreign Exchange Market and Net Exports

subtopics.title: Changes in the Foreign Exchange Market and Net Exports

outcomes.text: Explain how currency value changes alter net exports and aggregate demand.
Show that appreciation lowers exports, raises imports and cuts net exports.
Show that depreciation raises exports, lowers imports and lifts net exports.

topics.title: 6.6 Real Interest Rates and International Capital Flows

subtopics.title: Real Interest Rates and International Capital Flows

outcomes.text: Explain how real interest rate differences across countries affect capital flows and related markets.
Show financial capital flowing to the country with the higher real rate.
Explain that central banks influence domestic rates and so net capital inflows.
